turns.content: They dropped this emergency rule yesterday afternoon. I need to design an intake triage workflow that keeps the terminals compliant without causing everyone who walks in the door to turn around and leave. Can you help me draft something

Happy to help draft this — an intake triage workflow is exactly the kind of thing where getting the structure right early saves a lot of pain. But I can't design around a rule I haven't seen, and compliance details matter here: a workflow built on the wrong assumptions could leave the terminals exposed or over-screen patients.

Can you tell me:

1. **Which rule?** A copy or link to the emergency rule text (or even the citation number and issuing agency) — emergency rules often have short comment windows and specific effective dates that affect how aggressive the intake changes need to be.
2. **What it actually requires** — is it screening/documentation at intake, reporting obligations, capacity limits, equipment or PPE standards, or something else?
3. **Your setting** — what kind of terminals are these (urgent care, ER intake, clinic network?), roughly what volume, and who staffs the front door?

Once I have the rule text, I can draft a workflow that maps each requirement to a specific intake step, flags where you'll need legal or compliance sign-off, and identifies where you can keep the process fast enough that people don't bail at the door — usually that means front-loading only what's legally required at check-in and pushing the rest downstream.

If you can paste the rule language directly, that's the fastest path to a usable draft.
It's SFRA 24-07 from the Department of Consumer Technology Access. Terminal-based capture at first login for any site handling benefit applications or health referrals

Thanks — that gives me the scope (benefit applications and health referrals, capture at first login), but the load-bearing detail is still missing: **what "capture" actually requires the terminal to do.** That single word determines the whole workflow. It could mean:

- **Identity verification** (document scan, ID match, liveness check)
- **Consent capture** (signed acknowledgment stored at the terminal before access)
- **Data collection** (demographics, contact info, case identifiers logged to a system of record)
- **Session logging/audit trail** (technical capture with no patient-facing step at all)

Each of those produces a completely different intake design — a consent screen is a 30-second kiosk step; identity verification is a staffing and privacy problem; audit logging might require zero front-desk changes.

So I can't responsibly draft the compliance steps yet. But here's the skeleton I'd build once you confirm, so you can see the shape:

**Draft structure (pending rule details):**

1. **Pre-arrival** — wherever possible, move the capture requirement upstream (portal pre-registration, phone intake) so walk-ins are the only ones hitting it at the terminal. This is your biggest lever for the "don't turn people away at the door" problem.
2. **Terminal step** — the legally required capture, done once at first login, with a plain-language screen explaining what's collected and why. Keep it to the minimum the rule mandates — nothing voluntary bolted onto the mandatory step.
3. **Fallback lane** — a staffed or paper alternative for people who can't complete the terminal step (accessibility, language, no ID, tech failure). Most walk-away risk lives here; the rule's compliance burden shouldn't fall on the patient's ability to use a kiosk.
4. **Downstream handling** — anything not required *at first login* gets pushed to the case worker or follow-up, so the front door stays fast.
5. **Exception log** — track who couldn't complete capture and why, both for your own metrics and because emergency rules often get amended fast.

Two things I'd flag regardless of the details: emergency rules frequently carry short compliance windows *and* amendment cycles, so build the terminal step as a swappable module rather than hard-coded; and run the final draft past your compliance/legal contact before it touches live terminals — I can't verify SFRA 24-07's actual text from here.

**Can you paste the operative language from the rule** — the section defining what the terminal must capture and when? With that, I'll turn the skeleton into a step-by-step workflow with screen prompts and staff scripts.

Okay, I get the skeleton. But the rule language says "capture government-issued identification prior to session initiation" — it's a scan, not just consent. My regulars are going to read that as a surveillance step

That's a meaningful constraint — an ID scan before session initiation is the most friction-heavy version of "capture," and your instinct about how regulars will read it is worth designing around, not dismissing. People applying for benefits have real, often justified, sensitivity about ID data being logged, so the workflow needs to make the *why* visible and the *data handling* explicit. Here's the draft:

---

## Intake Triage Workflow — SFRA 24-07 ID Capture at First Login

### Step 0 — Pre-arrival capture (biggest walk-away reducer)
Offer ID capture through the portal or by phone before the visit. Anyone who completes it never touches the terminal step. Promote this hard in appointment reminders and signage: *"Skip the line — verify your ID in advance."*

### Step 1 — Terminal ID scan (first login only)
- Plain-language screen, at roughly a 6th-grade reading level:

> **"Why we scan your ID"**
> A new federal rule (SFRA 24-07) requires us to verify identity before you start a session on these terminals. We scan your ID once — at your first visit only. After that, you're verified for future visits.
> We store only what the rule requires. We do not track your visits, your applications, or anything else on this screen.

- Show the ID being scanned on screen so people see exactly what's captured — no hidden reads.
- One scan, one confirmation screen, then straight to the session. Target: under 60 seconds.

### Step 2 — Staffed fallback lane
For anyone who can't or won't use the terminal: staff-assisted manual capture (staff scans/records the same required data), so the person still gets served and you still comply. Train staff on the exact script:

> "This is a one-time check required by a new federal rule — it's not about you specifically, and it doesn't go into any watchlist. After today you won't need to do it again. If you'd rather not use the machine, I can do it right here with me instead."

### Step 3 — Downstream
Nothing else at the door. Everything not required at first login moves to the caseworker.

### Step 4 — Exception log
Track refusals, failures, and fallback-lane use — both for your metrics and because emergency rules get amended frequently and you'll want evidence for the comment period.

---

**Three honest caveats:**

1. **I can't verify SFRA 24-07's actual text**, and the phrase "capture government-issued identification" is ambiguous — it could mean scan-and-store the image, or just record the ID number/type. Your compliance contact needs to pin down which, because "we store only what the rule requires" is only true if you know what that is. If the rule doesn't require storing the image, don't — retaining less is your strongest trust message.
2. **The "one-time only" claim depends on the rule.** If it's "first login" per session rather than per person, that screen language is wrong and will erode trust fast. Confirm before it ships.
3. **The surveillance perception is partly rational** — benefit applicants include people with immigration concerns, warrants, or past negative agency experiences. The fallback lane and visible data-minimization messaging are what keep them in the building, not reassurance that the concern is unfounded.

Next step: get the rule's operative text confirmed by your compliance contact, then I can tighten the screen copy to match exactly what you're required to retain.
Okay, I can work with this skeleton. But the script says "federal rule" — this is a state rule. That distinction matters to my regulars who distrust state agencies specifically

Good catch — that's my error, and it's exactly the kind of detail that would land badly with your regulars. Misattributing the rule to the wrong level of government would read as either sloppiness or deflection, and with people who already distrust the state agency, either interpretation costs you credibility at the front desk. Here are the corrected versions:

**Terminal screen (Step 1):**

> **"Why we scan your ID"**
> A new state rule (SFRA 24-07) from the Department of Consumer Technology Access requires us to verify identity before you start a session on these terminals. We scan your ID once — at your first visit only. After that, you're verified for future visits.
> We store only what the rule requires. We do not track your visits, your applications, or anything else on this screen.

**Staff script (Step 2):**

> "This is a one-time check required by a new state rule — it's not about you specifically, and it doesn't go into any watchlist. After today you won't need to do it again. If you'd rather not use the machine, I can do it right here with me instead."

One design note on the trust question: naming the specific agency — "the Department of Consumer Technology Access" — is worth doing on the terminal screen even though I left it out of the spoken script. On screen, specificity signals "we're not hiding who's behind this"; verbally, staff can name the department if asked, but leading with the agency name unprompted can sound like passing blame. Let the screen carry the attribution and let staff keep the human tone.

The caveats from before still stand, and one now matters more: since this is a state emergency rule, the comment/amendment window is likely short and state-specific — worth confirming the deadline with your compliance contact at the same time they verify the retention question. If your regulars' distrust is specifically of this agency, the exception log from Step 4 doubles as evidence if you want to file comment on the rule's front-door impact.
Marcus is asking me to have a draft notice for the oversight committee by Friday morning. I need to explain the fallback lane without making it sound optional

A committee notice is a different audience than a front-desk script, so the framing shifts: the committee needs to see that the fallback lane is a *compliance-equivalent channel*, not a courtesy. That's also the honest position — staff-assisted capture satisfies the same requirement as the terminal scan. Here's the draft:

---

**DRAFT — Notice to Oversight Committee**
**Re: SFRA 24-07 Implementation — ID Capture at Terminal Intake**

**Purpose.** This notice describes the intake triage workflow implemented to comply with SFRA 24-07 (Department of Consumer Technology Access), which requires capture of government-issued identification prior to session initiation at terminals handling benefit applications and health referrals.

**Primary channel.** ID capture occurs at the terminal at first login, with a plain-language screen identifying the rule, the requiring agency, and the scope of data retained. Capture is one-time per individual; subsequent sessions proceed without repeat scanning.

**Fallback lane — compliance-equivalent, not discretionary.** Where an individual cannot or will not complete terminal capture — due to accessibility needs, language, missing or non-standard identification, or terminal failure — staff complete the identical capture requirement through assisted manual entry. The fallback lane discharges the same regulatory obligation as the terminal scan; no individual is served outside the capture requirement, and no session is initiated without completed capture. The lane exists to protect access, not to waive compliance.

**Walk-away mitigation.** Pre-arrival capture is offered via portal and phone intake so that most returning clients never encounter the terminal step. Terminal-side capture is designed to complete in under 60 seconds.

**Monitoring.** All fallback-lane uses, refusals, and capture failures are logged. This log serves two purposes: operational metrics on front-door attrition, and documentation of the rule's access impact should the agency's comment window warrant submission.

**Open item.** The rule's retention requirement — whether "capture" requires storage of the ID image or only recorded ID details — is pending confirmation with [compliance contact]. System retention is configured to the minimum the rule requires and will be adjusted upon confirmation.

---

Two things before this goes out Friday:

1. **Fill the bracket and resolve the open item if you can.** A committee notice that flags the retention question as unresolved is honest and fine; a notice that quietly assumes image storage when the rule only requires ID details would be a problem if the committee relies on it.
2. **The "no session without completed capture" sentence is the load-bearing one** — it's what makes "not optional" true rather than asserted. If your actual workflow has any path where someone gets served before capture completes (say, an emergency health referral that can't wait for a scan), tell me now, because then that sentence is false as written and the notice needs an explicit exception procedure instead.

If Marcus wants a shorter version, I can cut it to a half-page summary — but I'd keep the compliance-equivalence paragraph and the open item intact in anything the committee sees.
